title: Stargazing in NGC 6355
caption: The globular cluster NGC 6355, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6355 · constellation Ophiuchus · about 50000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, E. Noyola, R. Cohen

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Stars cover this Hubble view from edge to edge. Toward the center they crowd into an even denser circular region that also looks bluer, while redder foreground stars sit around the edges and many small stars fill the background. This is NGC 6355, a globular cluster less than 50,000 light-years away in Ophiuchus.

NGC 6355 lives in the inner regions of the Milky Way. Globular clusters are stable, tightly bound groups of tens of thousands to millions of stars. Their crowding and mutual gravity give them a roughly round shape, with a bright core fading into an ever sparser sprinkling of stars. Hubble captured this cluster's dense core in sharp detail.

From above the blurring of Earth's atmosphere, Hubble has transformed the study of globular clusters. From the ground, telling their stars apart is almost impossible, but Hubble lets astronomers examine them one by one.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.14 x 1.85 arcminutes) and distance (50000 light years), the frame spans roughly 46 × 27 light-years. Its light set out about 50,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The image combines blue, visible and near-infrared data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Hubble's position above the atmosphere lets it separate stars that would blur together for any eye or ground telescope, and one filter records near-infrared light we cannot see.
